text.headline: India-linked extortion wave shakes B.C.'s Panjabi community
text.text: A 2025 shooting at a Panjabi-owned cafe in British Columbia became a flashpoint in a wave of extortions and violence that Canadian officials linked to Indian intelligence collusion with the Lawrence Bishnoi organized-crime network. The pattern intensified fears within the province's Panjabi and Sikh community of transnational repression on Canadian soil.

media.caption: A welcome sign for Surrey, British Columbia — representative image of the Lower Mainland community affected by the 2025 extortion wave.

sources.title: Kapil Sharma Cafe Shooting (Baaz)

text.headline: Severe floods overwhelm Panjab as Sikh volunteers lead relief
text.text: In September 2025, severe flooding submerged large parts of Panjab, with gurdwaras and community volunteers, including groups such as Khalsa Aid, filling the vacuum left by a slow official response. Baaz commentary framed the crisis and the seva that followed as a reflection of state neglect of Panjab.

media.caption: The logo of Khalsa Aid International, one of the relief organizations that led flood response efforts in Panjab in September 2025 — representative image, not a photograph of the floods.

sources.title: The Floods Should Radicalize Punjab (Baaz)

text.headline: Canada designates the Bishnoi gang a terrorist entity
text.text: On 29 September 2025, the Government of Canada listed the Lawrence Bishnoi gang as a terrorist entity. The RCMP described the network as a proxy used by the Government of India to carry out homicides, arsons, and extortion as part of transnational repression against Canadian Sikhs, a designation advocates called a partial victory.

media.caption: Badge of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the agency that described the Bishnoi network as a proxy for transnational repression — representative image, not a photograph of the designation announcement.

sources.title: Bishnoi Gang Terrorist Designation A Partial Victory (Baaz)

text.headline: Jagtar Singh Johal's prolonged detention highlights UK inaction
text.text: By late 2025, British Sikh citizen Jagtar Singh Johal remained detained in India years after his 2017 arrest, amid allegations of UK-India intelligence collusion. Baaz described his unresolved case as an example of Britain failing to protect one of its own citizens abroad.

media.caption: Jagtar Singh Johal, the British Sikh detained in India since his 2017 arrest.

sources.title: Jagtar Singh Johal: The British Citizen That Britain Has Forgotten (Baaz)

text.headline: Survey finds widespread anti-Sikh hate on 50th anniversary of Chaggar's murder
text.text: In mid-2026, a World Sikh Organization report found that a large majority of surveyed Sikhs had experienced anti-Sikh hate, released as the community marked 50 years since the racist murder of teenager Gurdip Chaggar in Southall. The findings prompted reflection on how little had changed in confronting anti-Sikh hostility across the diaspora.

media.caption: Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha in Southall, London, near where Gurdip Chaggar was murdered in 1976 — representative image of the community marking the 50th anniversary.

sources.title: The Model Minority Trap: Sikhs Can't Assimilate Our Way Out of Hate (Baaz)

persons.name: Guru Nanak Sahib
persons.profession: First Guru of Sikhi, Founder of the Faith
persons.bio:
Guru Nanak Sahib was born in 1469 at Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib in present-day Pakistan, and is revered as the founder of Sikhi and the first of the Ten Gurus. Rejecting the ritualism and social hierarchies of the surrounding traditions, he taught the oneness of the Creator (Ik Onkar) and the fundamental equality of all people regardless of caste, creed, or gender. His hymns form the opening of the Sikh scripture, beginning with the Mul Mantar and the Japji Sahib.

He undertook long journeys, the Udasis, travelling across South Asia and reportedly as far as Mecca and Baghdad, accompanied by his companion the Muslim musician Bhai Mardana. In his final years he settled at Kartarpur on the banks of the Ravi, where he established a working community organized around three principles: Nam Japna (remembrance of the divine), Kirat Karni (honest labour), and Vand Chhakna (sharing with others), and instituted the practice of langar, the communal free kitchen.

Before his passing in 1539 he chose his devoted disciple Bhai Lehna over his own sons to succeed him, renaming him Guru Angad and establishing the principle that Guruship passed to the most worthy rather than by heredity. His birth anniversary, Gurpurab, is the most widely celebrated date in the Sikh calendar.

gallery.caption: Portrait of Guru Nanak in an oval frame
'Bhai Mardana, Guru Nanak, Sri Chand, Bhai Bala and Lakmi Chand', a Janamsakhi painting from a Kashmiri manuscript, early 19th century
'Imaginary Meeting of Guru Nanak, Mardana Sahab, and Other Sikh Gurus' — the earliest known painting depicting all ten Sikh gurus together, probably from Hyderabad, ca.1780

persons.name: Guru Angad Sahib
persons.bio:
Guru Angad Sahib, born Bhai Lehna in 1504, became the second Sikh Guru in 1539 after Guru Nanak recognized his complete devotion and obedience. He is traditionally credited with popularizing and standardizing the Gurmukhi script, the writing system in which the Sikh scripture is recorded, thereby giving the community a distinct literary identity separate from Sanskrit and Persian learned traditions.

He collected the compositions of Guru Nanak and continued to develop the institution of langar, emphasizing physical fitness and wrestling among his followers. He established his centre at Khadur Sahib. Before his passing in 1552 he conferred the Guruship on the elderly and devoted Amar Das, again setting aside his own sons.

gallery.caption: Depiction of Guru Angad from a Guru Granth Sahib manuscript on Kashmiri paper, Patiala
Bahi Lehna (later Guru Angad) and his companions visit Baba Nanak
Fresco depicting Guru Angad, from Udasi Chitta Akhara in Amritsar

persons.name: Guru Amar Das Sahib
persons.bio:
Guru Amar Das Sahib assumed the Guruship in 1552 at an advanced age and led the community for more than two decades. He is remembered for deepening the institutional and social reforms of the early Panth, most famously by insisting that all visitors, including the Mughal Emperor Akbar, first sit and eat together in the langar before meeting him, using the community kitchen as a levelling instrument against caste distinctions.

He established his seat at Goindwal, where he had a baoli (stepwell) constructed as a place of pilgrimage, and organized the growing community into administrative districts known as manjis. He spoke against the practices of sati and purdah, advocated the remarriage of widows, and composed the Anand Sahib. He appointed his son-in-law Ram Das as his successor.

gallery.caption: 18th century painting of Guru Amar Das
Depiction of Guru Amar Das from a Guru Granth Sahib manuscript on Kashmiri paper, Patiala
Fresco depicting Guru Amar Das, from Udasi Chitta Akhara in Amritsar

persons.name: Guru Ram Das Sahib
persons.profession: Fourth Guru of Sikhi, Founder of Amritsar
persons.bio:
Guru Ram Das Sahib became the fourth Guru in 1574. He is credited with founding the city that would become Amritsar, excavating the sacred pool (sarovar) around which the Harimandar Sahib would later be built, giving the Sikh world its central sacred geography.

He composed the Lavan, the four hymns that constitute the Sikh marriage ceremony (Anand Karaj), still recited at Sikh weddings today. Departing from earlier practice, he named his youngest son Arjan as his successor, beginning a hereditary line that would continue through the remaining Gurus.

gallery.caption: Equestrian painting of Guru Ram Das, accompanied by an attendant carrying a red flag, Punjab, circa early 19th century
Guru Ram Das (the fourth Sikh Guru), from a series of paintings of the first nine Sikh gurus, circa 1800–1840
Depiction of Guru Ram Das from a Guru Granth Sahib manuscript on Kashmiri paper, Patiala

persons.name: Guru Arjan Sahib
persons.profession: Fifth Guru of Sikhi, First Martyr, Compiler of the Adi Granth
persons.bio:
Guru Arjan Sahib, the fifth Guru from 1581, was one of the most consequential figures of the Guru period. He completed the construction of Harimandar Sahib at Amritsar, designing it with entrances on all four sides to signify openness to all peoples, and in 1604 he compiled the Adi Granth, the first authoritative volume of Sikh scripture, gathering the hymns of the preceding Gurus together with those of Hindu and Muslim Bhagats such as Kabir, Namdev, Ravidas, and Sheikh Farid.

He organized systems of community contribution, including the daswandh (a tenth of one's earnings), and during the Lahore famine of 1595 established langar and dug wells as acts of unconditional service. Under his leadership the Sikh community grew into a large and self-conscious body.

In 1606, on the orders of the Mughal Emperor Jahangir, Guru Arjan was tortured and martyred at Lahore, becoming the first of the Sikh Gurus to be martyred. His death is regarded as a turning point that set the community on the path toward taking up arms in defence of conscience.

gallery.caption: Depiction of Guru Arjan from a Guru Granth Sahib manuscript on Kashmiri paper, Patiala
'A Sikh Guru (Perhaps Guru Arjan Dev) Seated in the Golden Temple at Amritsar', Guler school painting, circa 1830 (traditionally identified as Guru Arjan, though attribution uncertain)
Contributors of the Guru Granth Sahib depicted with Guru Arjan while Bhai Gurdas scribes the Granth Sahib

persons.name: Guru Hargobind Sahib
persons.profession: Sixth Guru of Sikhi, Architect of Miri-Piri
persons.bio:
Guru Hargobind Sahib became the sixth Guru in 1606 following the martyrdom of his father, Guru Arjan. In response, he formally combined spiritual and temporal authority by donning two swords representing Miri (temporal power) and Piri (spiritual authority), and by establishing the Akal Takht Sahib, the Timeless Throne, facing the Harimandar Sahib at Amritsar as a seat of Sikh sovereignty.

He raised a standing armed force, the Akal Sena, and fought several defensive battles against Mughal forces. Imprisoned for a time in the fort at Gwalior, he is remembered in tradition for securing the release of fellow princely captives, an event commemorated as Bandi Chhor Divas. His transformation of the community into one prepared to defend itself with arms laid the groundwork for the militant Khalsa that followed.

A miniature painting of Guru Hargobind
Contemporary equestrian painting of Guru Hargobind, held in the collection of the Sodhi family of Kartarpur, circa mid-17th century

persons.name: Guru Har Rai Sahib
persons.bio:
Guru Har Rai Sahib, a grandson of Guru Hargobind, became the seventh Guru in 1644. He is remembered for his gentleness and compassion, maintaining a large cavalry force as a deterrent while avoiding direct conflict, and for his interest in medicine and healing, establishing gardens and a dispensary.

He navigated the tense politics of the Mughal succession struggle between Aurangzeb and Dara Shikoh with caution. When his elder son Ram Rai altered a line of scripture to appease the Mughal court, the Guru disowned him and instead named his younger son, Harikrishan, as his successor.

gallery.caption: Guru Har Rai (the seventh Sikh Guru), from a series of paintings of the first nine Sikh gurus, circa 1800–1840
Court of Guru Har Rai
Equestrian painting of Guru Har Rai with two angelic figures above, Pahari style

persons.name: Guru Harikrishan Sahib
persons.bio:
Guru Harikrishan Sahib became the eighth Guru in 1661 at the age of five, the youngest to hold the office. Despite his youth he faced opposition from his elder brother Ram Rai and the pressures of the court of Emperor Aurangzeb, who summoned him to Delhi.

While in Delhi he is revered for tending to victims of a smallpox and cholera epidemic, ultimately contracting the disease himself and passing away in 1664 at the age of eight. The Gurdwara Bangla Sahib in Delhi marks the site associated with his service. Before his death he indicated his successor with the words 'Baba Bakala,' pointing to Guru Tegh Bahadur.

gallery.caption: Guru Har Krishan (the eighth Sikh Guru), from a series of paintings of the first nine Sikh gurus, circa 1800–1840
Detail of Guru Har Krishan from a miniature painting depicting him conversing with a Hill Raja, circa early 19th century
Guru Har Krishan being worshipped by his followers

persons.name: Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib
persons.profession: Ninth Guru of Sikhi, Martyr for Freedom of Conscience
persons.bio:
Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib, the youngest son of Guru Hargobind, became the ninth Guru in 1664. He travelled extensively across northern and eastern India spreading Sikh teachings and founded the town of Anandpur Sahib in the Shivalik foothills in 1665. His compositions were later incorporated into the Guru Granth Sahib.

He is most revered for his martyrdom: when a delegation of Kashmiri Pandits sought his help against forced conversion under Aurangzeb, he took up their cause in defence of the freedom of conscience of a community not his own. He was arrested and beheaded in Delhi in 1675 after refusing to convert to Islam. The Gurdwaras Sis Ganj (Delhi) and Rakab Ganj mark the sites of his execution and cremation. His sacrifice in defence of another faith's right to worship is widely held to be without parallel.

gallery.caption: Contemporary painting of Guru Tegh Bahadur by Ahsan, ca.1667–68 (detail)
A 19th century painting depicting Guru Tegh Bahadur
Guru Tegh Bahadur (the ninth Sikh Guru), from a series of paintings of the first nine Sikh gurus, circa 1800–1840

persons.name: Guru Gobind Singh Sahib
persons.profession: Tenth Guru of Sikhi, Creator of the Khalsa
persons.bio:
Guru Gobind Singh Sahib, born at Patna in 1666, became the tenth and final human Guru in 1675 after the martyrdom of his father, Guru Tegh Bahadur. In 1699, at Anandpur Sahib on Vaisakhi, he created the Khalsa, initiating the first Panj Piare (Five Beloved) through the Khande di Pahul ceremony and giving initiated Sikhs the shared names Singh and Kaur along with the discipline of the Five Ks.

A poet, scholar, and warrior, he fought numerous battles against Mughal and hill-state forces. In the campaigns of 1704 he lost all four of his sons: the two elder Sahibzade, Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh, fell at Chamkaur, while the two younger, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, were bricked alive at Sirhind. His mother, Mata Gujri, also died in captivity.

He compiled the final recension of the Sikh scripture and, before his passing at Nanded in 1708 from wounds inflicted by an assassin, he ended the line of human Gurus by conferring eternal Guruship upon the Guru Granth Sahib. He also commissioned Banda Singh Bahadur to carry the Khalsa's struggle into Panjab.

gallery.caption: Portrait of Guru Gobind Singh seated on a square armless chair, leaning against a red bolster
'Guru Gobind Singh on Horseback', artist of the Guler-Kangra schools, early 19th century
An Equestrian Portrait of Guru Gobind Singh

persons.name: Banda Singh Bahadur
persons.profession: Khalsa Commander, Founder of the First Khalsa Raj
persons.bio:
Banda Singh Bahadur, born Lachman Dev and later an ascetic known as Madho Das, was transformed into a Khalsa warrior after meeting Guru Gobind Singh at Nanded in 1708. The Guru commissioned him to lead the Khalsa against Mughal oppression in Panjab, sending him north with a small band and letters of authority (hukamnamas) to the Sikhs.

In 1710 he defeated the Mughal faujdar Wazir Khan at the Battle of Chappar Chiri and captured Sirhind, establishing the first sovereign Khalsa Raj. He minted coins and issued edicts in the name of the Gurus, established a new capital, and enacted land reforms abolishing the zamindari system and granting cultivators rights to the land they worked.

After years of resistance he was besieged, captured, and taken to Delhi, where in 1716 he was tortured and executed along with hundreds of his companions after refusing to renounce his faith. His brief sovereignty is regarded as a foundational precedent for later Sikh rule.

gallery.caption: Banda Singh Bahadur mural fresco
Gilded panel from Takht Hazur Sahib, Nanded, depicting Madho Das (later known as Banda Singh Bahadur) declaring himself Guru Gobind Singh's 'Banda'
Silver rupee coin struck in Banda Singh Bahadur's name at the Amritsar mint, dated AD 1711 — a numismatic artifact, not a portrait

persons.name: Bhai Tara Singh Van
persons.bio:
Bhai Tara Singh of the village of Van (Vaan) in the Amritsar region was an early-eighteenth-century Sikh warrior remembered as one of the significant martyrs of the period following Banda Singh Bahadur's execution. He resisted the exactions and harassment of local officials of the Lahore administration.

He died fighting a large Mughal force sent against him in 1726. His martyrdom is cited as an early episode in the sustained cycle of persecution and resistance that galvanized the Sikh Panth through the eighteenth century.

gallery.caption: 19th-century Sikh drawing depicting Zakariya Khan, the Mughal governor of Lahore whose forces besieged and killed Bhai Tara Singh at the village of Van in 1726 — a depiction of his persecutor, not a portrait of Tara Singh Van himself, for whom no contemporary likeness is known to survive

persons.name: Jassa Singh Ahluwalia
persons.profession: Supreme Leader (Sultan-ul-Qaum) of the Sikh Misls
persons.bio:
Jassa Singh Ahluwalia was one of the foremost leaders of the misl period, when the Sikhs were organized into confederated fighting bands. As a young man he took part in the daring nighttime raids of 1739 that freed women and captives from the retreating army of Nadir Shah after the sack of Delhi.

He rose to command the Ahluwalia misl and was acclaimed leader of the Dal Khalsa, earning the title Sultan-ul-Qaum ('king of the nation'). He led the community through the massacres of the mid-century, including the Vadda Ghallughara of 1762, and struck coinage asserting Sikh sovereignty after Sikh forces captured Lahore.

His leadership through decades of genocidal campaigns helped consolidate Sikh territorial power across Panjab and prepared the ground for the sovereign rule later achieved under Maharaja Ranjit Singh. He died in 1783.

gallery.caption: Equestrian painting of Jassa Singh Ahluwalia, Punjab Plains, circa 1859
Equestrian painting of Jassa Singh Ahluwalia on horseback in front of his haveli with a fly-whisk attendant, circa late 18th century
Print of a painting of Jassa Singh Ahluwalia, as published in the Mahan Kosh (1930)

persons.name: Maharaja Ranjit Singh
persons.bio:
Ranjit Singh, leader of the Sukerchakia Misl, captured Lahore in 1799 and over the following years unified the fractured Sikh misls into a single sovereign state, the Sarkar-i-Khalsa, being proclaimed Maharaja in 1801. His empire eventually stretched from the Khyber Pass to Kashmir and Multan, governed as the last major indigenous power in the subcontinent before British paramountcy.

He modernized his army, the Khalsa Fauj, along European lines, employing foreign officers and building a formidable artillery, while commanders such as Hari Singh Nalwa secured the volatile North West Frontier. His rule was noted for its relative religious pluralism, employing Hindus, Muslims, and Europeans in high office, and he took the Koh-i-Noor diamond into his treasury.

He died in 1839. The succession disputes and court intrigues that followed his death fatally weakened the empire, which fell to the British within a decade. His reign is remembered as a high point of Sikh sovereignty.

gallery.caption: Portrait of Maharaja Ranjit Singh seated and holding an arrow, with smallpox facial scars visible, ca.1850
'Young Maharaja Ranjit Singh', Company style painting, 19th century
A portrait of Ranjit Singh, Maharaja of the Punjab, by Emily Eden, London, circa 1844

persons.name: Hari Singh Nalwa
persons.profession: Commander-in-Chief of the Sikh Khalsa Army
persons.bio:
Hari Singh Nalwa was the most celebrated general of Maharaja Ranjit Singh's Khalsa Army and commander-in-chief on the North West Frontier. He led the conquest and administration of frontier regions including Kasur, Multan, Kashmir, and Peshawar, and was renowned for halting the centuries-long pattern of invasions into the subcontinent through the Khyber Pass.

He built and garrisoned a chain of forts, including Jamrud at the mouth of the Khyber, to hold Afghan forces at bay. In 1837 he was killed at the Battle of Jamrud while defending the fort against a large Afghan army. His death removed one of the empire's most formidable commanders and is regarded as a serious blow to its frontier security.

gallery.caption: Depiction of Hari Singh Nalwa telling prayer beads. Sikh school, Punjab Plains, ca.1840–1845
General Hari Singh Nalwa on an elephant with his retinue, 1825–35
Oil painting of Hari Singh Nalwa displayed in the Lahore Museum

persons.name: Maharani Jind Kaur
persons.profession: Last Queen and Regent of the Sikh Empire
persons.bio:
Maharani Jind Kaur, the youngest wife of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, became regent in 1843 for her young son Maharaja Duleep Singh amid the succession crisis that followed her husband's death. A capable and determined political figure, she was regarded by the British as a formidable adversary, and colonial officials nicknamed her the 'Rebel Queen.'

After the Anglo-Sikh Wars and the annexation of Panjab, the British separated her from her son, imprisoned her, and exiled her, fearing her influence over Sikh resistance. She eventually escaped to Nepal and was reunited with Duleep Singh in England late in her life. She died in London in 1863, and her memory endures as a symbol of the last independent Sikh sovereignty.

gallery.caption: Miniature portrait of Maharani Jind Kaur
Maharani Jind Kaur, the mother of Maharaja Duleep Singh. Gouache and ivory, Punjab, circa mid-19th century
Maharani Jind Kaur. Watercolour by a Company artist, Punjab, ca.1865

persons.name: Maharaja Duleep Singh
persons.profession: Last Maharaja of the Sikh Empire
persons.bio:
Duleep Singh, the youngest son of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, became the last Maharaja of the Sikh Empire as a young child, with his mother Jind Kaur as regent. Following the British annexation of Panjab in 1849, he was deposed at the age of ten, separated from his mother, and made to surrender the Koh-i-Noor diamond to Queen Victoria.

Taken into British guardianship and converted to Christianity, he was exiled to England, where he lived as a country gentleman and became a favourite of Queen Victoria. Later in life he sought to reclaim his heritage and his throne, reconverting to Sikhi and unsuccessfully attempting to return to Panjab and rally support. He died in relative poverty in Paris in 1893, an emblematic figure of colonial dispossession.

gallery.caption: A bust-length portrait of the Maharaja Duleep Singh, depicted in profile, by Franz Xaver Winterhalter, dated 15 July 1854
'Maharaja Duleep Singh and Attendants', by Helen Catherine Douglas Mackenzie, Lahore, Punjab, 30 November 1849
Cabinet photograph of Duleep Singh, by John Mayall, 1859

persons.name: Bhai Maharaj Singh
persons.bio:
Bhai Maharaj Singh was a Sikh leader who organized armed resistance against the British annexation of Panjab during and after the Anglo-Sikh Wars. Regarded as one of the earliest organizers of anti-colonial revolt in the region, he attempted to rally forces to restore Sikh sovereignty before being captured by the British in 1849.

Deemed too dangerous to hold in Panjab, he was deported: on 15 May 1850 the ship Mohammad Shah carried him and his associate Kharag Singh from Calcutta to Singapore, where he was imprisoned. He died in confinement there in 1856, having lost his sight and health. He is honoured as an early martyr of the anti-colonial struggle, and his memory is preserved by the Sikh community in Singapore.

gallery.caption: Painting of the Sikh warrior Bhai Maharaj Singh, holding court in his darbar
Bhai Maharaj Singh and companion Khurruck Singh in a prison cell
Mural depicting Bhai Maharaj Singh and Baba Suraj Singh, from a Nirmala Sikh temple (Gurdwara Baba Bir Singh) at Naurangabad, Punjab

persons.name: Bhai Vir Singh
persons.profession: Poet, Scholar, and Leader of the Singh Sabha Movement
persons.bio:
Bhai Vir Singh was a poet, scholar, theologian, and reformer who became a leading figure of the Singh Sabha movement, the reformist and revivalist current that reshaped Sikh identity, literature, and institutions under colonial rule. He is often called the 'Sixth River of Panjab' for his towering influence on modern Panjabi letters.

Through novels, epic poetry, exegesis of scripture, and journalism, including the Khalsa Samachar, he worked to renew Sikh consciousness and distinctiveness in the face of Christian missionary and Hindu reformist pressures. He is widely regarded as a founder of modern Panjabi literature. He died in 1957.

gallery.caption: Photograph of Sikh literati Bhai Vir Singh in his younger days
Bhai Vir Singh with his spouse and his brother Dr Balbir Singh standing at back
Photograph of Sikh literati Bhai Vir Singh practicing yoga

persons.name: Kartar Singh Sarabha
persons.bio:
Kartar Singh Sarabha was a young revolutionary who became one of the most prominent figures of the Ghadar Party, founded in 1913 among Panjabi and Sikh immigrants on the west coast of North America to organize armed rebellion against British rule in India. As a student in California he helped edit the party's Ghadar newspaper.

He returned to India to foment an uprising among Indian soldiers, but the plot was uncovered. Tried in the Lahore Conspiracy Case, he was hanged in 1915 at the age of nineteen. He became an iconic martyr of the anti-colonial movement and a personal inspiration to later revolutionaries, notably Bhagat Singh.

gallery.caption: Photograph of Ghadar Party revolutionary Kartar Singh Sarabha
Photograph/print of Kartar Singh Sarabha

persons.name: Bhai Mewa Singh
persons.bio:
Bhai Mewa Singh Lopoke was a Sikh immigrant in British Columbia active in the community's struggle against discriminatory Canadian immigration laws around the time of the Komagata Maru affair. Amid intimidation of the Sikh community by informants working for the colonial and Canadian authorities, he shot and killed William Hopkinson, an immigration inspector and intelligence agent, at the Vancouver courthouse in 1914.

He made no attempt to escape and framed his act as a defence of his community and faith. He was hanged on 11 January 1915. He is honoured as an early shahid (martyr) of the diaspora Sikh community, commemorated annually in British Columbia.

gallery.caption: Portrait painting of Bhai Mewa Singh Lopoke, Ghadar-era Sikh martyr in British Columbia

persons.name: Private Buckam Singh
persons.bio:
Buckam Singh was a Sikh immigrant to Canada who enlisted and fought for the Canadian Expeditionary Force during the First World War, despite immigration laws of the era that barred people of South Asian origin from the country. He served in Flanders, was wounded, and contracted tuberculosis.

He died in a military hospital in Kitchener, Ontario, in 1919. His resting place is the only known grave of a First World War Sikh Canadian soldier in Canada, and his story has become a focus of Remembrance Day commemoration of the Sikh contribution to Canadian and Allied war efforts.

gallery.caption: Photograph of Sikh-Canadian soldier Buckam Singh with a group of Sikh men, ca.1907–1915
Detail of Buckam Singh, cropped from a group photograph of Sikh men, ca.1907–1915
Newspaper clipping photograph of Buckam Singh, Toronto Telegram, 1915

persons.name: General Reginald Dyer
persons.bio:
Colonel (acting Brigadier-General) Reginald Dyer was the British Indian Army officer who ordered troops under his command to open fire on an unarmed crowd gathered at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar on 13 April 1919, during Vaisakhi. The firing continued until ammunition was nearly exhausted, killing hundreds and wounding many more in an enclosed space with few exits.

The massacre became one of the defining atrocities of British colonial rule. Dyer was censured by the Hunter Commission and removed from command, though he was lauded by sections of the British public. He died in 1927.

gallery.caption: Press photograph of General Reginald Dyer, distributed by the Central News agency, London, 1919
The Jallianwala Bagh memorial in Amritsar, built to commemorate the victims of the 1919 massacre Dyer ordered — a representative image of the site, not a photograph of Dyer himself
Inscribed quote from General Dyer at the Jallianwala Bagh site, Amritsar — a documentary/memorial photograph, not a portrait of Dyer

persons.name: Michael O'Dwyer
persons.bio:
Sir Michael O'Dwyer served as Lieutenant-Governor of Panjab from 1913 to 1919 and endorsed General Dyer's actions at the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, presiding over the harsh repression and martial law that followed across the province. He remained an unrepentant defender of the massacre for the rest of his life.

He was assassinated in London on 13 March 1940 by Udham Singh, who held him responsible for the atrocity. He died at Caxton Hall more than two decades after the events at Amritsar.

gallery.caption: Photograph of Maharaja Brij Indar Singh of Faridkot State seated with Sir Michael O'Dwyer, the Lieutenant-Governor of Punjab, ca.1916
Front-page headline from The Daily Telegraph reporting on the assassination of Michael O'Dwyer by Udham Singh, 14 March 1940 — a newspaper document, not a photo of O'Dwyer

persons.name: Shaheed Bhagat Singh
persons.bio:
Bhagat Singh, born into a Panjabi Sikh family with a strong nationalist heritage, became one of the most influential revolutionaries of the Indian independence movement. Inspired in part by the Ghadar martyr Kartar Singh Sarabha, he embraced militant and socialist ideas through the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association.

He took part in the killing of a British police officer in retaliation for the death of the nationalist leader Lala Lajpat Rai, and in the throwing of non-lethal bombs in the Central Legislative Assembly as a symbolic protest, courting arrest to publicize revolutionary ideas. Tried and convicted, he was hanged by British authorities on 23 March 1931 at the age of twenty-three. He is remembered as a martyr claimed across the political spectrum in South Asia and within the lineage of Panjabi anti-colonial resistance.

gallery.caption: Detail of Bhagat Singh, from a photograph of him in jail, 1927
Portrait of Bhagat Singh at the age of seventeen, ca.1924–25
Photograph of Bhagat Singh at the age of ten, ca.1917–18

persons.name: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi
persons.profession: Leader of the Indian Independence Movement
persons.bio:
Mohandas Gandhi was the pre-eminent leader of the Indian independence movement, known for his philosophy of non-violent resistance (satyagraha). In the context of Sikh history he is a contested figure: in August 1936 he published an article in his journal Harijan labelling a proposed mass conversion of so-called 'untouchables' to Sikhi 'A Dangerous Proposal,' a stance many Sikhs read as revealing anxieties over caste, conversion, and Sikh distinctiveness in late colonial India.

He was assassinated in 1948. His statements and positions on Sikh questions have remained points of critical discussion in Sikh political and historical writing.

gallery.caption: Portrait photograph of Mohandas K. Gandhi, 1930s
Studio photograph of Mahatma Gandhi, London, 1931

persons.name: Udham Singh
persons.bio:
Udham Singh was a Panjabi revolutionary who assassinated Sir Michael O'Dwyer, the former Lieutenant-Governor of Panjab, at Caxton Hall in London on 13 March 1940, in retribution for O'Dwyer's endorsement of the 1919 Jallianwala Bagh massacre, which Udham Singh is said to have witnessed. He had waited more than two decades to carry out the act.

He was tried in Britain and hanged in 1940. Associated with the Ghadar tradition and revolutionary networks, he adopted the composite name Ram Mohammad Singh Azad to symbolize religious unity. Sikh writers have criticized later film and media portrayals for erasing his Sikh identity and the religious dimension of his motivations.

gallery.caption: Photograph of Udham Singh
Detail of Udham Singh, cropped from a group photograph of Sikhs gathered for Guru Nanak's birth anniversary at Gurdwara Shepherd's Bush, London, 1937

persons.name: Sirdar Kapur Singh
persons.profession: Sikh Scholar, Civil Servant, and Parliamentarian
persons.bio:
Sirdar Kapur Singh was a scholar, former Indian Civil Service officer, and parliamentarian who became one of the most influential Sikh political theorists of the twentieth century. Dismissed from the civil service in circumstances he attributed to anti-Sikh bias, he turned to writing and Panth politics, earning the honorific 'National Professor of Sikhism.'

In the aftermath of the 1947 Partition he articulated one of the clearest theoretical cases for a distinct Sikh homeland within postcolonial India, grounding it in Guru Gobind Singh's vision of the Khalsa and in what he described as Sikh grievances against the Indian state, expressed in documents such as the 'Betrayal of the Sikhs.' His writings shaped later debates over Sikh autonomy and the Anandpur Sahib Resolution. He died in 1986.

gallery.caption: Photograph of Sardar Kapur Singh from his time as an Indian Civil Service (ICS) officer
Parliament House (Sansad Bhavan), New Delhi, where Kapur Singh served as a parliamentarian — a representative image of the institution, not a photograph of Kapur Singh himself

persons.name: Indira Gandhi
persons.bio:
Indira Gandhi served as Prime Minister of India for most of the period from 1966 to 1984. In 1975 she imposed a nationwide Internal Emergency, suspending civil liberties and jailing opponents; Sikh organizations mounted one of the most sustained resistance campaigns against it, with large numbers courting arrest.

In June 1984 she ordered Operation Blue Star, the Indian Army assault on the Harimandar Sahib complex in Amritsar, which killed large numbers of pilgrims and severely damaged Sikhism's holiest site, becoming a central trauma of modern Sikh history. On 31 October 1984 she was assassinated by two of her Sikh bodyguards in apparent retaliation for the assault. Her killing was followed within hours by organized anti-Sikh violence across Delhi and northern India.

Indira Gandhi at a banquet in Vancouver during a state visit, The Province, 1949
Nehru with Indira Gandhi at the Sikh temple in Vancouver, The Province, 1949

persons.name: Sant Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale
persons.bio:
Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale was the leader of the Damdami Taksal, an influential Sikh seminary, and became a pivotal and highly contested figure in the Sikh movement of the late 1970s and early 1980s. Rising to prominence amid disputes with the Sant Nirankari sect and broader grievances over Panjab's autonomy, river waters, and religious rights, he became a rallying point for a militant assertion of Sikh identity.

In a widely cited 1982 speech in Bombay he rejected offers of state police protection, saying his only protector was the Guru and the Sangat. In the months before June 1984 he took up residence within the Harimandar Sahib and Akal Takht complex amid an escalating confrontation with the Indian government.

He was killed during Operation Blue Star in June 1984. He remains a deeply polarizing figure, regarded by many Sikhs as a martyr and defender of the faith and by the Indian state and its supporters as a militant, a division that continues to shape debates over the period.

gallery.caption: Photograph of Sant Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale.

Handwritten Guru Granth Sahib manuscript struck by a bullet during Operation Blue Star, 1984 — a representative image of the event that ended Bhindranwale's standoff at the Darbar Sahib, not a photograph of him (no free-licensed photograph of Bhindranwale could be confirmed on Wikimedia Commons)
The Golden Temple (Harmandir Sahib) complex in Amritsar, site of the Darbar Sahib standoff and Operation Blue Star in 1984 — a representative location image, not a portrait of Bhindranwale

persons.name: Talwinder Singh Parmar
persons.bio:
Talwinder Singh Parmar was a Canada-based Sikh militant and founder of the Babbar Khalsa organization. A public inquiry in Canada later concluded that he was the mastermind of the June 1985 bombing of Air India Flight 182, which killed all 329 people aboard, most of them Canadian citizens, in the deadliest act of aviation terrorism prior to 2001.

He was never convicted in relation to the bombing; a Canadian criminal prosecution of others largely failed, and the affair was marked by catastrophic failures of Canadian security agencies. Parmar returned to India, where he was killed by Panjab police in 1992 in disputed circumstances. His role remains central to Canadian discussion of the Air India tragedy.

gallery.caption: Memorial to the victims of the Air India Flight 182 bombing (1985), an attack a Canadian public inquiry concluded was masterminded by Talwinder Singh Parmar — a representative memorial image, not a photograph of Parmar himself

persons.name: Gurdip Singh Chaggar
persons.bio:
Gurdip Singh Chaggar was an eighteen-year-old Sikh student killed in a racially motivated attack in Southall, west London, in June 1976. His murder became a catalyzing moment for Sikh and South Asian youth in Britain, galvanizing the formation of the Southall Youth Movement and a broader anti-racist mobilization.

His death is remembered as a landmark in the history of the British South Asian struggle against racist violence. On its fiftieth anniversary in 2026, community organizations reflected on how much anti-Sikh and anti-South Asian hostility persisted.

gallery.caption: Photograph of Gurdip Singh Chaggar.

Representative image of a Sikh gurdwara — no free-licensed photograph of Gurdip Singh Chaggar could be confirmed on Wikimedia Commons; his 1976 racist murder in Southall, London, is documented mainly through press-agency photographs that are not freely licensed

persons.name: Beant Singh
persons.bio:
Beant Singh was a Congress politician who became Chief Minister of Panjab after the 1992 state election, held amid a widespread Sikh boycott. His government is held by Sikh rights advocates to have overseen a campaign of extrajudicial killings and enforced disappearances of Sikh youth during the counter-insurgency of the early 1990s, later documented by the human rights defender Jaswant Singh Khalra.

He was killed on 31 August 1995 in a suicide bombing at the Panjab civil secretariat in Chandigarh, carried out by Dilawar Singh, with Balwant Singh Rajoana convicted as a conspirator. Sikh accounts frame the killing as retribution sought for the bloodshed of the counter-insurgency years.

gallery.caption: 2013 Indian commemorative postage stamp bearing the likeness of Beant Singh, Chief Minister of Punjab (1992–1995) — a stamp portrait, not a photograph

persons.name: Jaswant Singh Khalra
persons.bio:
Jaswant Singh Khalra was a human rights defender who exposed the scale of the Indian state's counter-insurgency campaign in Panjab. Investigating municipal cremation records, he documented thousands of secret and illegal police cremations of Sikh youth who had been abducted, extrajudicially killed, and disposed of as 'unidentified' bodies.

After publicizing his findings internationally, he was abducted by Panjab police in September 1995 and murdered while in custody. Years later several police officials were convicted in connection with his killing. He is revered as one of the Panth's most respected modern martyrs and a symbol of the struggle for accountability for the disappearances of the 1980s and 1990s.

gallery.caption: Photograph of Jaswant Singh Khalra, the human rights activist who exposed extrajudicial killings and illegal cremations by Punjab Police

persons.name: Yogi Bhajan (Harbhajan Singh Puri)
persons.bio:
Harbhajan Singh Puri, known as Yogi Bhajan, was the founder of the 3HO ('Healthy, Happy, Holy Organization') and Sikh Dharma movement in the United States from 1969, introducing a form of Kundalini yoga and gathering a following of largely white American converts to a version of Sikhi. He built a network of businesses, schools, and institutions.

Beginning in 2022, the Siri Singh Sahib Corporation, successor to his organization, acknowledged decades of abuse and announced a reparations program for survivors, following accounts by former members. Subsequent investigative reporting in 2024 detailed neglect and abuse suffered by American children sent to 3HO boarding schools in India from the 1980s, deepening critical scrutiny of his legacy. He died in 2004.

Photograph of Yogi Bhajan meeting Pope John Paul II

persons.name: Justin Trudeau
persons.bio:
Justin Trudeau served as Prime Minister of Canada from 2015 to 2025. His official visit to India in February 2018 became mired in controversy amid media allegations linking Canadian Sikh politicians to 'separatists,' a narrative Sikh commentators traced through years of skewed coverage of Sikh political activity in Canada.

In September 2023 he announced to the House of Commons that Canadian agencies were pursuing credible allegations linking agents of the Government of India to the June 2023 assassination of Hardeep Singh Nijjar in British Columbia, triggering a major diplomatic rupture between Ottawa and New Delhi, which rejected the allegations. His government's later actions, including the terrorist designation of the Bishnoi network, further shaped Canada-India relations over transnational repression.

Photograph of Justin Trudeau, 2021

persons.name: Deep Sidhu
persons.profession: Actor and Activist, Founder of Waris Punjab De
persons.bio:
Deep Sidhu was a Panjabi actor who became a prominent activist voice during the 2020-2021 Farmers' Protest. He was among those accused in connection with the January 2021 Republic Day incident at the Red Fort in Delhi, where a Nishan Sahib was raised, an episode that drew intense controversy.

He founded the organization Waris Punjab De to champion Panjab's rights and identity. On 15 February 2022 he died in a car crash on a highway near Delhi, a death many Sikhs regarded as suspicious. His funeral drew a large gathering with prominent displays of support for Khalistan, and leadership of his organization later passed to Amritpal Singh.

gallery.caption: Photograph of Deep Sidhu (born Sandeep Singh Sidhu), actor and founder of Waris Punjab De.
The Red Fort (Lal Qila), Delhi — site of the 26 January 2021 Republic Day tractor rally incident in which Deep Sidhu was implicated; a representative location image, not a photograph of Sidhu himself

persons.name: Sidhu Moose Wala (Shubhdeep Singh Sidhu)
persons.bio:
Shubhdeep Singh Sidhu, known as Sidhu Moose Wala, was an internationally successful Panjabi singer, rapper, and songwriter who also entered politics as a Congress candidate. His music addressed Panjabi identity, rural life, and social themes, earning him a vast following across Panjab and the diaspora.

On 29 May 2022 he was shot dead in Panjab, a day after his state-provided security detail was reduced. His killing, later linked to organized-crime networks including the Lawrence Bishnoi gang, shocked the Panjabi diaspora. His posthumously released track 'SYL,' addressing Panjab's river-water dispute, became a protest anthem.

Photograph of Sidhu Moose Wala during a 2019 interview
Sidhu Moose Wala during the shooting of his film Moosa Jatt

persons.name: Amritpal Singh Sandhu
persons.profession: Sikh Preacher, Leader of Waris Punjab De, Member of Parliament
persons.bio:
Amritpal Singh Sandhu emerged as a Sikh preacher and activist who, following Deep Sidhu's death, was formally appointed leader of Waris Punjab De in a ceremony at Rode village in September 2022. Adopting the style and rhetoric of Sant Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale, he led a rapid Amrit Sanchar and anti-drug revival campaign that drew both large followings and government alarm.

In February 2023 his supporters stormed the Ajnala police station near Amritsar demanding an associate's release. In March 2023 Panjab police launched a sweeping crackdown, imposing a statewide internet blackout, and after weeks evading capture he was arrested in April 2023 and detained without trial under the National Security Act in Assam's Dibrugarh jail.

While still detained, in June 2024 he won the Khadoor Sahib parliamentary seat as an independent with over 400,000 votes, a result Sikh commentators called a striking rebuke to claims that pro-Khalistan sentiment lacks support in Panjab.

Representative image of a Sikh gurdwara in Punjab — no free-licensed photograph of Amritpal Singh Sandhu could be confirmed on Wikimedia Commons at time of writing

persons.name: Parmjit Singh Panjwar
persons.bio:
Parmjit Singh Panjwar was a Pakistan-based Sikh activist and chief of a faction of the Khalistan Commando Force, long designated a militant by Indian authorities. He had lived in Pakistan for decades.

On 6 May 2023 he was shot dead by unidentified gunmen near Lahore. His killing was one of several sudden deaths of Khalistan-linked figures within a few weeks in mid-2023, which Sikh writers described as part of a coordinated global campaign later corroborated by Western investigations into Indian transnational operations.

gallery.caption: Photograph of Parmjit Singh Panjwar.

A landmark in Lahore, Pakistan, the city where Parmjit Singh Panjwar lived for decades in exile and was assassinated in 2023 — a representative location image, not a photograph of Panjwar himself (no free-licensed photograph of him could be confirmed on Wikimedia Commons)

persons.name: Avtar Singh Khanda
persons.bio:
Avtar Singh Khanda was a prominent UK-based Khalistan activist associated with organizing and advocacy in Britain. He came to wider attention around the 2023 events surrounding Amritpal Singh and Waris Punjab De.

On 15 June 2023 he died suddenly in Birmingham. His family and Sikh organizations considered the circumstances suspicious, and UK police and coroners were later accused of failing to properly investigate allegations that he had been poisoned. His death, days before the killing of Hardeep Singh Nijjar, is cited in discussions of alleged transnational repression targeting Sikh activists abroad.

gallery.caption: Photograph of Avtar Singh Khanda.

Guru Nanak Gurdwara Smethwick, near Birmingham — the UK Midlands region where Avtar Singh Khanda was based as a Sikh diaspora activist and where he died in 2023; a representative location image, not a photograph of Khanda himself (no free-licensed photograph of him could be confirmed on Wikimedia Commons)

persons.name: Hardeep Singh Nijjar
persons.profession: Sikh Separatist Leader and Gurdwara President
persons.bio:
Hardeep Singh Nijjar was a Canadian Sikh community leader, president of the Guru Nanak Sikh Gurdwara in Surrey, British Columbia, and an advocate for the Khalistan movement, including support for the Sikhs for Justice referendum campaign. India had designated him a terrorist, an accusation his supporters rejected as politically motivated.

On 18 June 2023 he was shot dead in the parking lot of his Surrey gurdwara. A later US indictment described how an Indian government employee coordinated the killing with an intermediary, and in September 2023 Canada's Prime Minister stated that Canadian agencies had credible evidence linking agents of India to the assassination, which India rejected as absurd. His killing became the central case in international scrutiny of alleged Indian transnational repression of Sikhs.

gallery.caption: Photograph of Hardeep Singh Nijjar, 2020

persons.name: Nikhil Gupta
persons.profession: Indian National Charged in Assassination Plot
persons.bio:
Nikhil Gupta is an Indian national arrested in Prague on 30 June 2023 at the request of United States authorities and later extradited to the US. American prosecutors accused him of directing, on behalf of an Indian government employee, a foiled plot to assassinate the Sikh American activist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun on US soil.

The US Justice Department publicly detailed the case in an unsealed indictment in November 2023, which also indicated the plot's connection to a target in Canada shortly before Hardeep Singh Nijjar's killing. He has pleaded not guilty, and the case remains a focal point of US scrutiny of alleged Indian transnational repression.

gallery.caption: The U.S. Department of Justice, which charged and prosecuted Nikhil Gupta over the foiled assassination plot — a representative institutional image, not a photograph of Gupta himself (no free-licensed photograph of him could be confirmed on Wikimedia Commons)

persons.name: Gurpatwant Singh Pannun
persons.profession: Attorney and Founder of Sikhs for Justice
persons.bio:
Gurpatwant Singh Pannun is a Sikh American (and Canadian) attorney and the general counsel and co-founder of Sikhs for Justice (SFJ), the group that organizes the non-binding Khalistan Referendum votes held across the diaspora from 2022. A vocal advocate for an independent Khalistan, he has been designated a terrorist by India, a designation his supporters characterize as an attack on peaceful advocacy.

In 2023 US federal prosecutors alleged that an Indian government employee had directed a foiled plot to assassinate him on US soil, detailed in the indictment of Nikhil Gupta. The case became a landmark in international scrutiny of alleged Indian transnational repression.

gallery.caption: Map of the proposed state of 'Khalistan' as circulated by Sikhs for Justice, the organization founded and led by Gurpatwant Singh Pannun — a representative document, not a photograph of Pannun himself (no free-licensed photograph of him could be confirmed on Wikimedia Commons)

persons.name: Jagtar Singh Johal
persons.bio:
Jagtar Singh Johal is a British Sikh citizen from Dumbarton, Scotland, and a blogger and activist who documented Sikh human-rights issues. He was arrested in Panjab in November 2017 while visiting for his wedding and has since been held in prolonged detention in India, facing charges his supporters and human-rights organizations say are unfounded, amid allegations that he was tortured to extract a confession.

By late 2025 he remained detained years after his arrest, amid allegations that UK intelligence-sharing contributed to his detention. Sikh writers and campaigners describe his unresolved case as an example of Britain failing to protect one of its own citizens abroad, and it has become a prominent cause in UK Sikh advocacy.

gallery.caption: Photograph of Jagtar Singh Johal.

The Palace of Westminster, London — the UK Parliament has repeatedly debated and raised Jagtar Singh Johal's detention in India; a representative institutional image, not a photograph of Johal himself (no free-licensed photograph of him could be confirmed on Wikimedia Commons)

persons.name: Lawrence Bishnoi
persons.bio:
Lawrence Bishnoi is an imprisoned Indian gangster whose organized-crime network has been linked to a wave of violence affecting the Panjabi diaspora. His gang was implicated in the May 2022 killing of the singer Sidhu Moose Wala and, according to Canadian authorities, in a 2025 wave of extortions and shootings in British Columbia.

In September 2025 the Government of Canada listed the Lawrence Bishnoi gang as a terrorist entity, with the RCMP describing the network as a proxy used by the Government of India to carry out homicides, arsons, and extortion as part of transnational repression against Canadian Sikhs. He has remained in Indian custody throughout, directing operations from prison according to investigators.

mahmood-1996.author: Cynthia Keppley Mahmood
